readerTitle: How Blockbuster filled its shelves by changing how studios got paid
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Blockbuster와 영화 스튜디오의 1998년 수익 배분 계약), 실제 연구 (Mortimer 2008, Cachon & Lariviere 2005), 가상 적용 (인테리어 시공, 급여 소프트웨어)
insight: 수익 배분 비율은 단순한 가격이 아니라 누가 위험을 지는지를 정하는 결정이다. 배분의 기준, 비율, 기간이 숫자보다 중요하다.
misconception: 파트너 계약에서 중요한 것은 공정한 비율 하나뿐이다. 이익을 나누는 것이 매출을 나누는 것보다 항상 공정하다.

sources.text: Cachon, G. P. & Lariviere, M. A. (2005). Supply Chain Coordination with Revenue-Sharing Contracts: Strengths and Limitations. Management Science, 51(1).
Mortimer, J. H. (2008). Vertical Contracts in the Video Rental Industry. Review of Economic Studies, 75(1).
가상 사례 (인테리어 시공사와 디자이너, 급여 소프트웨어와 회계법인)의 수치는 모두 설명용

factChecks.note: 테이프 한 개당 약 $65(기존), 약 $8(수익 배분 후 선불), 스튜디오 몫 약 40%는 Cachon & Lariviere(2005)에 나오는 대략적 수치입니다. 스튜디오와 작품마다 조건이 달랐으므로 카드에 "reportedly", "around"로 적었습니다. 원문에서 다시 확인하세요.
Blockbuster가 수익 배분 계약을 맺은 시기(1998년)와, 그 결과 신작 재고가 크게 늘었다는 내용을 1차 자료로 확인하세요.
Mortimer(2008)가 수익 배분이 스튜디오와 대여점 양쪽의 이익을 높였다고 결론 내렸는지, 작품 유형별 차이가 있는지 원문에서 확인하세요. 카드에는 "tended to raise profits for both"로 일반화해 적었습니다.
Rentrak이 소규모 대여점의 수익 배분 계약에서 대여 기록을 추적하는 역할을 했다는 내용을 확인하세요.

cards.title: How Blockbuster filled its shelves by changing how studios got paid
body: In the mid-1990s, a new movie on videotape could cost a rental store around $65 a copy. Stores bought a handful and hoped for the best. On Friday nights, customers often found the hit they wanted already gone.
In 1998, Blockbuster fixed its empty shelves without paying more for tapes. It changed how the movie studios got paid.

image.label: Empty new-release shelf with one lonely videotape
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 1990년대 비디오 대여점의 'New Releases' 선반이 거의 비어 있고 테이프 한 개만 남아 있음. 실망한 손님 실루엣. 실제 Blockbuster 로고, 영화 제목, 스튜디오 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A designer wants to send you clients.
body: You renovate kitchens and bathrooms. A local interior designer offers to refer clients. Jobs range from a $5,000 bathroom refresh to an $80,000 full kitchen.
How do you pay the designer?

options.text: A flat $500 for every client who signs
options.feedback: Simple and easy to track. But the designer earns the same for a $5,000 job as an $80,000 one, so there's no reason to send you the big ones.

options.text: 5% of the job price, paid when the client pays you
options.feedback: The designer earns more on bigger jobs, and you only pay from money you've actually received. Your cost rises and falls with the work.

options.text: 20% of your profit on each job
options.feedback: It sounds fair, but the designer can't see your costs. Every job turns into an argument about what counts as profit.

cards.title: The old deal put all the risk on the store.
body: Under the old model, the store paid the studio in full, up front. If a movie flopped, the store absorbed the loss. So stores bought cautiously, and popular titles ran out.
Blockbuster's new deals flipped this. It paid a much lower price per tape and gave the studio a **share of every rental**.
With cheap tapes, Blockbuster could stock many more copies of each new release. The studio now earned money every time a tape went out, not just when it was sold.

cards.title: Same tape, two deals.
body: Exact terms varied by studio and title. These are the rough figures reported by researchers who studied the deals.

breakdown.label: Old deal: price per tape
breakdown.detail: Paid up front. The store kept all rental income.

breakdown.label: New deal: price per tape
breakdown.detail: A small payment up front, reportedly under $10

breakdown.label: New deal: studio's share
breakdown.detail: Reportedly the studio's cut of each rental

cards.title: Revenue sharing
body: **Revenue sharing** means paying a partner a percentage of the money your joint work brings in, instead of a fixed price.

The percentage is more than a price. It decides **who carries the risk**. A fixed fee puts the risk on the buyer. A share spreads it: the studio earned more on hits and less on flops, and Blockbuster stopped paying full price for tapes nobody rented.
Economist Julie Mortimer later studied these contracts and found they tended to raise profits for both studios and stores.

image.label: Seesaw of risk shifting from store to shared
image.brief: 두 장면 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Fixed price': 시소 한쪽에 대여점만 무거운 'Risk' 상자를 짊어짐. 오른쪽 'Revenue share': 대여점과 스튜디오가 'Risk' 상자를 함께 들고 있음. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Three choices shape every revenue share.
body: The percentage gets the attention, but three other decisions matter as much.
list: **The base:** revenue or profit. Revenue is easy for both sides to check. Profit depends on costs only one side can see.
**The split:** roughly what each side brings. The studio brought the movie. The store brought shelves, staff and customers.
**The length:** one sale, the first year, or for as long as the customer stays.
cards.callout: Settle these three, and the percentage becomes the easy part.
cards.softwareNote: App stores, marketplaces and reseller programs all run on revenue shares. The base and length matter as much as the rate: 20% of the first year is a very different deal from 20% for life.

cards.title: You have to count it, and you might overpay.
body: A share only works if both sides trust the numbers. Studios needed records of every rental. Many smaller stores worked through Rentrak, a company that tracked rentals for revenue-sharing deals.
A share also pays out more when things go well. If success is nearly certain, a fixed fee may be cheaper.
And a partner paid on revenue doesn't feel your costs. They may push discounts or small, messy jobs that earn them a cut but lose you money.

cards.title: Now it's payroll software.
body: You sell payroll software to small businesses for $100 a month. Customers who fit well usually stay for years.
An accounting firm with 300 small-business clients wants to recommend you. Which offer do you make?

options.text: A one-time $300 bonus for each new customer
options.feedback: Predictable for you. But the firm earns nothing once a client signs up, so it has little reason to send good fits or help them stay.

options.text: 20% of each customer's monthly fee, for as long as they stay
options.feedback: The firm earns $20 a month only while the client keeps paying, so it wants clients who stick. You pay from revenue you've already collected.

options.text: 50% of every monthly fee, to win the firm's loyalty
options.feedback: The firm will love it, but half of every payment leaves for good. Check that what's left still covers serving the customer.

cards.title: A revenue share decides who carries the risk.
body: Before arguing over the percentage, settle the base, the split and the length, and make sure both sides can count the money.
**Try it today:** list what you pay partners or suppliers. Which fixed fees would work better as a share? Which shares would be cheaper as a fixed fee?
